title: A nephew's warning (Acts 23)
hookLine: Paul's sister's son overhears an ambush plot and tells the commander
tomorrow: a governor hears about self-control and says: not now…

lines: A CHAT HE WASN'T MEANT TO SEE.
cards: Somebody's little brother sees a group chat he wasn't meant to see, and something in it is about a person you love. Does he say anything?
In Jerusalem, a band of men swear an oath not to eat or drink until they've killed Paul; Acts says there were more than forty of them. And who overhears? Acts never gives his name or his age.

teach.b: Today's question: where does courage come from when you're being hunted? Acts gives two answers.
The first comes the night before, in the fortress: "the Lord stood by him, and said, Be of good cheer, Paul." Today's line, take heart, is that phrase in plainer words. The second answer is a person.
"And when Paul's sister's son heard of their lying in wait, he went and entered into the castle, and told Paul."

teach.h: A NEPHEW WALKS IN TO TELL.
teach.b: Paul sends him to the commander, who "took him by the hand, and went with him aside privately, and asked him, What is that thou hast to tell me?" A powerful man, taking a young one by the hand.
That same night Paul rides out of Jerusalem under heavy guard.
Now a neighbor. Muslims remember a night of hiding too.

The Qur'an recalls the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in a cave with one companion while men searched for them, and his words to his frightened friend, in Pickthall's translation: "Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us."

Muslim tradition names the friend Abu Bakr, and the journey the Hijra. Here's the one to tell a friend tonight: in both stories, courage arrives in the dark as words, God is with you, before anyone is safe.

The honest difference: in Acts, Christians hear the risen Lord himself standing by Paul and speaking. In the Qur'an, the Prophet speaks the comfort to his friend, and the verse says God sent down his peace.

how: Christians read Acts 23 as part of Paul's road to Rome; some preachers point to the nephew when they speak about ordinary people who protect others by speaking up.

o: a letter warning Paul not to go to Rome
a prophet's sign about Paul's arrest
a young man who overheard a plot and spoke up

games.q: the plot and the warning — tap the pairs.
p: grieve not. lo! Allah is with us

s: an important official uncovered the plot against Paul
a young relative overheard it and walked into the castle to tell.
Acts tells us the nephew's name
he's only ever Paul's sister's son.
the commander told the nephew to keep it quiet
see thou tell no man that thou hast shewed these things to me.

games.q: a coworker mentions, half-joking, that a few people plan to blame the new hire for a mistake they made. the manager doesn't know. what fits Acts 23?
o: quietly tell the manager, who can actually act on it.
warn everyone in the break room so it can't happen.
stay out of it; it isn't your business to repeat.
games.why: the nephew took it to Paul, then to the commander, aside and privately: to the person who could act.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind someone who might need courage this week, or a warning that only you could pass on. Hold them there, and let two words rest on them: take heart. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: A nephew's warning. A young man with no name who overheard an ambush plot and walked into the fortress to tell.

orig.note: Greek: take heart, the word the King James gives as be of good cheer in Acts 23:11.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: take heart, Paul, words spoken in the dark before any rescue came. Go well.
